<ConflictType> — Conflicting opinions and research outcomes: evidence spans positive correlations, small effect sizes, and counterexamples

Evidence clusters show three perspectives: (1) meta-analyses and large MRI studies report a modest positive link between brain volume and intelligence [d3, d5]; (2) evolutionary and genetic narratives connect brain size expansion to cognitive changes but do not establish direct causation [d2, d1]; and (3) counterexamples and constraints—sex differences without intelligence differences, Einstein’s smaller brain with localized enlargements, and energetic trade-offs—undermine a simple size–intelligence link [d6, d7, d4]. There is no clear consensus on whether brain size directly determines intelligence. Meta-analyses and large MRI-based studies report a modest positive correlation between brain volume and cognitive performance, but the effect is small—explaining roughly 2% of variability in test scores [d3, d5]. Evolutionary and genetic accounts link increases in brain size to cognitive changes over time, yet they do not establish a direct causal link to intelligence [d2, d1]. Counterexamples further complicate the picture: men’s brains are about 10% larger than women’s on average, yet this size difference does not affect intelligence [d6]; Einstein’s brain was smaller overall but had localized enlargements tied to specific cognitive abilities [d7]; and larger brains impose energetic burdens and diminishing returns, limiting gains in intelligence from size alone [d4].
